description: Memory-retrieval eval corpus for Luna's memory bench. 200 fictional records (60 project, 40 preference, 60 episodic, 40 distractor) describing a fictional personal AI-assistant product's architecture, deploy machinery, desktop UI, background jobs, and its operator's standing preferences, plus dated 2026 episodic events. 230 queries across five slices: verbatim (near-copy of a record substring), paraphrase (same meaning, reworded, may share content words), vocab-mismatch (same meaning, zero shared content words with the target record - synonyms, hypernyms, or descriptions by effect), temporal (time-anchored questions resolved against episodic record dates, with 'now' assumed to be 2026-07-14), and negative (plausible questions with no correct record in the corpus, expecting an empty relevantIds). Distractor records share two or more distinctive words with a target record's text but mean something unrelated, and are never a relevantId for any query.

records.text: Luna's memory system stores embeddings in a local vectorlite HNSW index layered on top of bun:sqlite for fast approximate nearest-neighbor lookup.
Luna's hybrid search combines BM25 keyword scores and vector cosine scores using Reciprocal Rank Fusion to produce a single ranked list.
The memory MCP server exposes three tools to the agent: save, search, and delete, so the agent can manage its own persistent recall.
Luna runs a small local embedding model called the ember-mini encoder for memory vectors, avoiding a round trip to any external embedding API.
When a new memory is saved with cosine similarity above 0.92 to an existing entry, the memory router merges them instead of creating a duplicate.
Every memory entry carries a kind tag of project, preference, or episodic so retrieval can bias ranking toward the category the query implies.
The memory export tool dumps all entries to a single JSON file for backup, independent of the live sqlite database.
Episodic memory entries carry a 180 day soft expiry; entries not reinforced by a later reference are excluded from default search after that window.
Luna ships to two deploy channels, stable and dev, so risky changes can soak in dev before promotion to stable.
The autodeploy timer checks for active chat sessions before restarting a channel and defers the rollout rather than interrupting a live conversation.
Passing the allow-active flag to the autodeploy command forces a rollout even while sessions are active, for urgent fixes.
If a deploy fails its post-restart health check, the deploy pipeline automatically rolls the channel back to the previous known-good build.
The widget dock desktop app ships through a staged update train so a broken build can be halted before it reaches most installs.
Each deploy channel runs inside its own isolated sandbox pod, so the stable and dev channels never share a filesystem or process table.
Every change must pass the no-mistakes validation pipeline, which runs review, tests, and lint, before it can reach a deploy target.
Luna's backend services are wired together as composable Effect-TS layers, including the account broker, the session store, and the job ticker.
Luna keeps all of its local runtime state, including databases and account secrets, under a single hidden directory on the operator's machine.
The session store persists chat threads and their messages in sqlite, so a restart never loses conversation history.
When a chat client reconnects, the session store restores the last active thread per route but caps how many stale connections it will reattach.
New threads are automatically titled by reading the first user message and stripping any client-added marker line before deriving the title.
The sidebar hides threads that never received a real user message, so probe and test threads no longer clutter the thread list.
Clicking the plus button spawns a brand new panel with a fresh thread, letting the operator run two conversations side by side.
Task-tool subagent runs are rendered inline in the chat timeline as their own collapsible turns.
The job ticker is Luna's second-generation background scheduler and fully replaced the original scheduler, which is no longer in the codebase.
Each background worker has its own configurable deadline and retry backoff, replacing a single global timeout that used to fail every job type the same way.
Background jobs run as bounded Effect fibers so the job ticker can cap concurrency and avoid overwhelming the host machine.
The nightly digest job compiles a summary of the day's activity and delivers it into a dedicated digest thread every morning.
When a background job finishes, its result is delivered directly into the chat thread that originally triggered it.
The observability service writes structured events as JSON Lines to a local event log for later analysis.
Cost accounting listens for spend events from the observability service and rolls them up per session, per team, and per workflow.
A watchdog process sends a heartbeat and pages the operator if a service enters a crash loop, with a manual restart lever as a fallback.
The event log can be queried directly with DuckDB, letting the operator run ad-hoc analysis over months of observability data without a separate database.
The account broker rotates OAuth tokens across several linked accounts to balance load and track the health of each one.
The vault backend stores secrets in the operating system's secure keychain where available, falling back to an encrypted directory on systems without one.
Agent permissions follow a broad allowlist paired with explicit deny rails, so agents get wide reach by default but cannot touch a short list of protected operations.
When an agent needs a secret from the operator, it requests one through a secure input field so the value never appears in the visible transcript.
The connector consent flow supports linking more than one account per provider, so the operator can switch which linked account a workflow uses.
The desktop app enforces a single running instance and registers a custom URL scheme so links can hand off directly into an existing window.
Skills are self-contained bundles of instructions and scripts that the agent can load on demand for a specific kind of task.
The connector system PRD describes three pillars: authentication, data sync, and the desktop panel surface that displays connected data.
MCP app panels let a connected tool render its own interactive surface directly inside a desktop widget panel.
The workflows gallery panel lists reusable multi-step workflows the operator can launch with a single click.
The nightly reflection job can propose improvements to existing skills, surfaced to the operator as review chips in chat.
Inbound Telegram photos and PDFs are queued per chat in a bounded FIFO and passed through a file-type sniff check before being attached to a thread.
The Telegram channel renders replies with formatted text, shows a typing indicator, and supports a small set of slash commands.
Voice replies are synthesized on-device using the operating system's built-in speech framework rather than a cloud text-to-speech service.
The attach-machine capability gives an agent full local shell access on the operator's machine rather than a folder-confined subset.
Luna's engineering workflow is trunk-based: every branch merges directly to the main branch and no long-lived secondary branch is kept around.
A migration study concluded that Luna's sqlite-based storage should coexist with a future Postgres-backed entities service rather than migrate wholesale.
Provider routing chains are keyed by a model identifier, so a single request can be routed to whichever provider currently serves that model.
The composer includes a switcher for choosing both the model and its reasoning effort before sending a message.
Font family and size for the chat interface are configurable from the settings panel and persist across restarts.
Desktop notifications are grouped into four categories so the operator can mute noisy categories without losing urgent ones.
The desktop app ships a soft watercolor visual theme as an alternative to the default light and dark themes.
Adjacent widget panels magnetically weld their edges together so dragging one panel can tow a connected cluster.
The whole widget dock can collapse into a single small orb icon and expand back out with a keyboard shortcut.
Generated artifacts of every supported kind can be opened and viewed directly inside a desktop panel instead of only in chat.
The desktop window's native close, minimize, and maximize buttons are given extra clickable padding so they register reliably near the window edge.
A staged liveness system escalates from a simple heartbeat to a crash-loop pager to a manual restart lever as failures get more severe.
A nightly reflection job, a beliefs file, and a periodic survey together form a closed loop that keeps the agent's stated preferences aligned with observed behavior.
Morgan Ellery prefers terse responses with no trailing recap; answer the question and stop.
Morgan Ellery prefers being addressed by full name rather than a shortened first name.
Morgan Ellery keeps the editor and terminal in dark mode at all times.
Morgan Ellery wants shell examples written in Zsh syntax by default, reserving Bash only for portable scripts and skills.
Morgan Ellery expects a claim to be checked, by running a command or reading a file, before it is stated as fact.
Morgan Ellery keeps most credentials in a password manager and treats the OS keychain as a fallback store.
Morgan Ellery prefers a fresh git commit over amending an existing one unless an amend is explicitly requested.
Morgan Ellery keeps daily notes and personal knowledge in a flat, metadata-tagged note vault.
Morgan Ellery wants interactive commands suggested with a leading exclamation mark so they can be run straight from the prompt.
Morgan Ellery's contact email for both work and personal matters is morgan.ellery@example.com.
Morgan Ellery never wants an em dash in written text; a plain hyphen should be used instead.
Morgan Ellery wants long markdown documents written with one full sentence per physical line.
Morgan Ellery does not want development cost weighed heavily in technical decisions, favoring quality, simplicity, and long-term maintainability instead.
Morgan Ellery insists that agents always work from a git worktree rather than editing a branch directly.
Morgan Ellery wants exploration and search work handed off to subagents so the main thread's context stays clean.
Morgan Ellery wants a short end-of-turn summary on shipped work covering what shipped, the risk, judgment calls made, and what's next.
Morgan Ellery wants a bug reproduced end-to-end, the way a real user would trigger it, before any fix is attempted.
Morgan Ellery is picky about visual polish and wants any obviously wrong UI detail fixed along the way, even if unrelated to the current task.
Morgan Ellery wants lint errors and flaky tests fixed on sight, even when they were not caused by the current change.
Morgan Ellery wants technical decisions backed by research and shown evidence rather than assumptions.
Morgan Ellery wants workflow scripts authored on a large model but has their subagents run on smaller models chosen by task difficulty.
Morgan Ellery does not want CHANGELOG files or other auto-generated files edited by hand.
Morgan Ellery expects a one-off, scoped instruction for the current task to override a standing preference without permanently changing that preference.
Morgan Ellery wants the operating instructions section of any guidance file left untouched unless they explicitly change how they want to work.
Morgan Ellery takes their coffee with oat milk and no sugar.
Morgan Ellery does not want emoji added to written output unless they specifically ask for it.
Morgan Ellery wants confirmation before any destructive git operation such as a force push or a hard reset.
Morgan Ellery wants agents to proceed without asking on reversible actions that clearly follow from the original request.
Morgan Ellery prefers native desktop notifications over in-app toast banners for anything urgent.
Morgan Ellery likes multi-key chord shortcuts for actions they use often, rather than single hotkeys that collide with other apps.
Morgan Ellery works on Pacific time and wants dates and schedules expressed in that zone unless stated otherwise.
Morgan Ellery wants commit messages that explain why a change was made rather than restating what the diff already shows.
Morgan Ellery never wants an agent's name added as a co-author on a commit.
Morgan Ellery prefers pull requests kept small and scoped to one concern rather than bundling unrelated changes.
Morgan Ellery wants any claim that has not been checked flagged as unproven rather than stated with confidence.
Morgan Ellery requires a real screenshot of any user-facing UI change before considering the change done.
Morgan Ellery wants throwaway scripts kept in a dedicated scratch folder rather than scattered through the main project tree.
Morgan Ellery never wants an agent to change its own permission configuration without being asked.
Morgan Ellery does not want any personal infrastructure details, like real hostnames or internal aliases, appearing in a public repository.
Morgan Ellery wants technical claims backed by a first-party, original source rather than a secondhand summary whenever one is available.
On 2026-01-08, the original scheduler was retired and the job ticker became the only scheduler running in production.
On 2026-01-15, the tiered vault backend shipped, adding keychain storage on systems that support it and an encrypted directory fallback everywhere else.
On 2026-01-22, provider routing chains keyed by model identifier were merged, closing the seam left open by the first routing pass.
On 2026-01-29, the first-run setup wizard for the desktop app was verified against a real build and shipped.
On 2026-02-03, on-device voice replies shipped after the speech framework integration cleared its verification pass.
On 2026-02-10, the physical string effect connecting satellite panels to the dock was rebuilt to survive a panel being dragged off-screen.
On 2026-02-17, the multi-provider routing seam went live, letting a single conversation switch providers mid-thread.
On 2026-02-24, a dead code sweep removed several unused modules, though one package was kept after a barrel-import check flagged it as still in use.
On 2026-03-02, native window buttons shipped after discovering the desktop framework's window command needed an explicit capability entry or the call was silently rejected.
On 2026-03-05, per-route last-thread restoration and a reattach cap shipped together to stop stale connections from piling up after a restart.
On 2026-03-09, a fix landed so widget panels only float above other windows when the operator has explicitly turned that setting on.
On 2026-03-13, a draft of the self-update command for the backend server was opened, covering the first phase of a planned four-phase rollout.
On 2026-03-18, the native window traffic light buttons were fixed by growing the titlebar hit area and adding a drag guard in the frontend.
On 2026-03-23, panel dragging lag was fixed by coalescing move events onto a single animation frame instead of applying each one immediately.
On 2026-03-27, a hard rule was adopted never to add a crisp ring or border outline to a widget's shell after a review flagged it as visually jarring.
On 2026-04-01, a bug where the streaming adapter silently swallowed an underlying failure cause was fixed and merged.
On 2026-04-06, the deploy router's multi-route slice merged, though SPKI pinning and a live rollout to the secondary connection pool were left for a follow-up.
On 2026-04-10, a race condition in the panel welding refresh was fixed by coalescing and debouncing the seam recalculation.
On 2026-04-14, a release looked broken only in the installed desktop app; the root cause turned out to be a stale webview cache that needed purging on every version change.
On 2026-04-17, parallel panel support shipped behind an access control list keyed to a per-panel identifier.
On 2026-04-21, the new React and Vite based companion web app replaced the older framework it was built to succeed.
On 2026-04-24, the Telegram channel upgrade shipped with formatted replies, a typing indicator, and a small set of slash commands.
On 2026-04-28, the default daily-driver model was switched to a faster mid-tier model, with a larger model kept available as an advisor option.
On 2026-05-02, clustered widget windows were made to tow each other using a native transient window attachment instead of a manual position sync.
On 2026-05-06, a desktop app release shipped the parallel panel access control list to every operator on the stable channel.
On 2026-05-08, a set of experimental widgets were verified live against the new web companion app after a local auth gap was worked around.
On 2026-05-11, a follow-up incident again traced a broken-looking release back to webview cache staleness, confirming the purge-on-version-change rule was necessary.
On 2026-05-14, the nightly digest job started failing with a deadline_passed error because every job type shared one global five minute timeout regardless of how long it actually needed.
On 2026-05-14, the digest job failure was traced to the scheduler's single global timeout rather than to the digest job's own logic, which was working correctly.
On 2026-05-18, an audit of a competing internal agent project found it had been dead since a clean-exit code path silently stopped it from restarting.
On 2026-05-21, per-worker deadlines and retry backoff merged to replace the single global timeout that had caused the digest job failure earlier that month.
On 2026-05-24, the per-worker deadline fix was deployed to both the dev and stable channels and the digest job began completing reliably again.
On 2026-05-27, a single-window thread switcher for the desktop app shipped, replacing an earlier cross-window redocking approach that proved unreliable in real use.
On 2026-05-29, automatic thread titling shipped, deriving a title from the first user message the first time a thread is read after creation.
On 2026-06-01, thread titling was hardened to strip a client-added marker line before deriving the title, after titles were found leaking that marker text.
On 2026-06-03, the nightly reflection job's prompt length problem was fixed in a sandboxed verification pass, cutting the token count enough to stop truncation.
On 2026-06-05, the reflection job's prompt fix was still pending a stable channel deploy with sample logging turned on to confirm the fix under a real overnight run.
On 2026-06-08, a change to hide empty and archived threads from the sidebar merged, using an existence check that runs before the row limit is applied.
On 2026-06-10, a spot check against a copy of the production thread database found that twenty-two of thirty-five threads had never received a real user message.
On 2026-06-13, the workflows gallery panel was put up for review after the dead in-chat workflow engine it replaced was fully removed.
On 2026-06-15, the first stage of the liveness ladder shipped as a draft, adding a watchdog heartbeat, a crash-loop pager, and a manual restart lever.
On 2026-06-17, the operator asked that any big refactor be preceded by a small throwaway spike that validates the underlying assumption first.

On 2026-06-19, an effort-level dropdown shipped, but the effort type turned out to be defined three separate times across the protocol, wire format, and reducer, so all three had to be widened together.
On 2026-06-22, a memory leak in the chat server's reattach path was fixed by adding a heartbeat and bounding the connection cache to five hundred and twelve entries.
On 2026-06-24, background job results began delivering directly into the thread that triggered them instead of only appearing in a separate results panel.
On 2026-06-27, the top bar of the desktop app was redesigned, and a rendering quirk was found where the embedded web view silently dropped a modern color function inside inline SVG icons.
On 2026-06-29, a public workspace notes file was found to be both publicly readable and directly injected into the agent's prompt, so deploy infrastructure details were removed from it.
On 2026-07-01, the operator clarified that workflow scripts should be authored on the largest available model but their subagents should run on a smaller model chosen for the task.
On 2026-07-02, the phase zero gate for the native companion app passed after it was verified running in a real embedded webview rather than a browser simulation.
On 2026-07-04, phase one of the native companion app merged, adding a transport layer, last-thread restoration, and an unbounded reconnect loop.
On 2026-07-06, custom URL deep linking and single-instance enforcement for the native companion app merged after the launch behavior was proven against a real build.
On 2026-07-08, the fix for silently dropped Telegram photo and PDF attachments was deployed and verified live against a real chat.
On 2026-07-09, the per-worker deadline fix was confirmed merged and deployed to both channels, closing out the root cause of the earlier May digest job failures.
On 2026-07-09, the thread sidebar decluttering fix was force-deployed to the stable channel, dropping the visible thread count from one hundred twenty one down to about sixty seven.
On 2026-07-09, phase two of the native companion app merged, adding real desktop notification banners across four categories.
On 2026-07-10, all five planned phases of the native companion app were marked complete, closing out a project that began with a phase zero spike.
On 2026-07-11, it was noted that updates to the workflow registry file require a full desktop app restart before the new entries appear in the gallery panel.
On 2026-07-12, build tooling timestamp files started being ignored by version control after they kept showing up as noise in every diff.
On 2026-07-13, the reflection job's skill-improvement proposals began surfacing to the operator as review chips directly in chat.
On 2026-07-14, a fresh worktree setup failure was traced to a shared package cache permission error, fixed by pointing the install command at a per-operator cache directory.
A bank vault is considered secure once its walls exceed a foot of reinforced concrete, regardless of the lock brand.
A car's spare keychain is often kept as a fallback in a kitchen drawer in case the everyday one goes missing.
A diary app calls each saved note a memory entry, though under the hood it is just a plain text file with no search index.
Memory foam mattresses ship compressed in a small box and slowly expand back to full size once the packaging is removed.
The human digestive system breaks down food using enzymes secreted by the stomach and small intestine.
A wooden boat dock needs its pilings inspected every few years for rot below the waterline.
A hospital review panel evaluates unusual medical cases and recommends a course of treatment.
Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity and are typically rated by their peak wattage output.
A tailor matches sewing thread to fabric weight so a seam doesn't pucker once it's pressed.
A subway token was once required for fare payment before contactless cards replaced the system entirely.
A runway model walks a designer's newest collection in front of a seated front row.
An architect builds a scale model of a building to show a client the massing before construction begins.
Dark roast coffee beans are roasted longer, producing a bolder flavor with less perceived acidity.
Push notification marketing campaigns see the highest engagement when sent during commute hours.
A junkyard watchdog is trained to patrol the fence line at night and bark at intruders.
A violin string typically needs replacing about once a year for a player who practices daily.
Metal welding joins two pieces of steel by melting a filler rod into the seam between them.
Drag racing measures how quickly a car covers a quarter mile from a standing start.
A movie's title sequence often sets the tone before the first line of dialogue is spoken.
A cache of cash hidden under a floorboard is a common trope in heist films.
A kitchen timer set for a soft-boiled egg usually reads about six minutes.
An airline boarding deadline typically closes fifteen minutes before a flight's scheduled departure.
A rail yard scheduler sequences which locomotive pulls out first during a shift change.
A trained singing voice can project across a concert hall without any electronic amplification.
A telegram sent in the early twentieth century charged by the word, which pushed senders toward terse phrasing.
A vector in physics has both a magnitude and a direction, unlike a plain scalar quantity.
A jeweler's gem embedding technique sets small stones directly into a metal band without visible prongs.
The Conventional Commits convention standardizes commit message prefixes like feat and fix across many open source projects.
Git worktrees let a developer check out multiple branches of the same repository into separate directories at once.
OAuth 2.0 access tokens should be short-lived and paired with a refresh token for any long-running session.
BM25 is the default keyword ranking function in Elasticsearch and performs well without any vector index at all.
A long exposure effect in photography blurs moving water into a smooth, silky texture.
A properly baked layer cake needs each layer to cool completely before it's stacked and frosted.
A wind-up widget sold at a novelty shop clicks and spins for about thirty seconds before it runs down.
Juggling three balls is usually the first skill a beginner performer learns before moving on to clubs or rings.
A plumbing connector fitting joins two pipes of different diameters without a full pipe replacement.
A court session can be adjourned by a judge if a key witness fails to appear.
A television channel's ratings are measured by the number of households tuned in during a given time slot.
A roller coaster's rollback safety feature stops the train from cresting a hill it doesn't have enough speed to clear.
A pager clipped to a belt was the standard way an on-call doctor got reached before mobile phones became common.
